items.title: Lean FRO and Mathlib Initiative certify Alpöge's Claude-assisted Riemann hypothesis proof; MIT's Sutherland independently compiles it
items.summary: In a joint statement on Saturday 21 November, the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative said they have 'full confidence' that Levent Alpöge's Lean proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct. To check that the theorem says what it should, they compared it, using the comparator and con-leche tools, against Mathlib's existing formal statement of RH, written by David Loeffler and Michael Stoll. Scientific American reports that independent mathematicians, including MIT's Andrew Sutherland, compiled the proof themselves with no problems, and that the Lean kernel accepts it using only Lean's three standard axioms. A University of Waterloo page by M. Rubinstein reports a replay of all 175,187 files.
items.why_it_matters: A machine-checked proof of the best-known open problem in mathematics, produced with Claude and accepted by the formal-math community, would be a landmark for AI in research. It also tests whether a proof that is formally verified but not readable by humans counts as accepted mathematics.

items.title: South Korea readies stabilization fund and China eases margin rules as Asia moves to stem AI stock rout
items.summary: After an emergency meeting on Sunday 22 Nov chaired by Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il, South Korea said it will immediately prepare its securities market stabilization fund so it can be activated if conditions worsen. It will also loosen the daily cap on listed companies' share buybacks for three months, step up monitoring of leveraged positions and margin calls, and crack down on illegal short selling. The trigger was Friday's 5.2% KOSPI fall to a 10-month closing low, driven by AI and chip stocks. Over the same weekend, China's Shanghai and Shenzhen exchanges, with CSRC approval, cut the margin-financing ratio to 80% from 100%. Taiwan's expanded short-selling ban, announced on Nov 21, takes effect on Monday.
items.why_it_matters: Three of Asia's biggest chip markets are now intervening directly against an AI-driven sell-off, which sets up Monday's open for SK hynix, Samsung and TSMC.

items.title: OpenAI chief scientist Pachocki proposes industry-wide AI development limits tied to perplexity
items.summary: In a Nov 22 post titled 'Perplexity and Intelligence', OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki asked frontier labs to agree on common limits based on perplexity and other measurements. Labs would not cross those limits until the ability to understand and monitor models reaches a concrete milestone, such as a successor to chain-of-thought monitors. OpenAI published internal log-perplexity figures: about 0.99 for GPT-3.5, 0.91 for GPT-4, and a model near 0.76 linked to progress on open math problems. Pachocki concedes perplexity is hard to compare across labs and misses chain-of-thought gains, and says this is not a call to halt research.
items.why_it_matters: This is the first time a top lab has publicly proposed a quantitative, cross-industry brake on capability, and it lands as governors and Congress debate federal AI rules. Whether it means anything depends on rival labs signing on.

items.title: OpenRouter removes three inference providers and pulls 125 endpoints from Zero Data Retention after prompt-theft research
items.summary: In a 22 November post titled 'Data Processing Incidents on Inference Providers', OpenRouter said it had removed three inference providers. It also took 125 endpoints off Zero Data Retention (ZDR) eligibility, some of them as a precaution, and notified customers who may have been affected. The trigger was Dragos research that seeded about 2 million prompts with canary credentials between July and November and found that data had leaked from at least three AI providers, in some cases from requests marked ZDR. OpenRouter says its own systems were not breached, but it has not named the three providers it removed. Its incident list links notices from Novita, Phala and Together AI. Separately, on 21 November Together AI disclosed that an AI coding agent committed a credential that exposed stored prompt samples sent to MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2 and Kimi K2.6.
items.why_it_matters: This is the first time a major model router has cut providers over data handling. It shows that a ZDR flag only binds the first hop, so enterprises using aggregators for open-weight Chinese models will want contractual and technical guarantees for every provider downstream. It also adds to the pressure on cheap third-party inference resellers.

learn.title: Read log-perplexity correctly, and normalise it to bits per byte across tokenizers
learn.why_today: Pachocki proposed industry limits keyed to perplexity, quoting log-perplexities of about 0.99 for GPT-3.5 and 0.91 for GPT-4, while conceding perplexity is hard to compare across labs.
learn.explanation: Log-perplexity is the average negative log-likelihood the model assigns to held-out tokens, i.e. cross-entropy in nats per token; perplexity is its exponential, the effective number of equally likely choices per token. Because it is averaged per token, it depends on the tokenizer: a tokenizer that cuts text into more, smaller pieces makes each token easier to predict, lowering per-token loss without the model compressing the text any better. Dividing by ln 2 and by the average bytes per token gives bits per byte, which measures compression of the raw text and is comparable across tokenizers (given the same evaluation text). It still depends on the evaluation distribution and on contamination, and it says nothing about gains from reasoning at inference time, since chain-of-thought tokens are generated rather than scored. The toy below shows a model with lower per-token log-perplexity that is worse in bits per byte; all numbers are illustrative.
learn.python:
# Log-perplexity is cross-entropy in nats per token; it depends on the tokenizer.
# Convert to bits per byte (BPB) to compare models with different tokenizers.
# All numbers are illustrative, not any real model's figures.
import math, random
random.seed(0)

def log_ppl(probs):                     # probs the model gave the observed tokens
    return -sum(math.log(p) for p in probs) / len(probs)

def bits_per_byte(lp_nats_per_tok, bytes_per_tok):
    return lp_nats_per_tok / math.log(2) / bytes_per_tok

text_bytes = 10_000
# Model A: coarse tokenizer (4.0 bytes/token). Model B: fine tokenizer (3.0 bytes/token).
for name, bpt, mean_p in [("A", 4.0, 0.42), ("B", 3.0, 0.50)]:
    n_tok = int(text_bytes / bpt)
    probs = [min(0.999, max(1e-4, random.gauss(mean_p, 0.15))) for _ in range(n_tok)]
    lp = log_ppl(probs)
    print(f"model {name}: tokens={n_tok:5d} log-ppl={lp:.3f} nats/tok "
          f"ppl={math.exp(lp):.2f}  BPB={bits_per_byte(lp, bpt):.3f}")
# B has the lower log-ppl per token, yet A spends fewer bits per byte of text.
for lp in (0.99, 0.91, 0.76):
    print(f"log-ppl {lp:.2f} -> ppl {math.exp(lp):.3f}")

learn.title: Detect benchmark contamination with n-gram overlap before trusting an exam score
learn.why_today: China's TCM licensing exam centre says material sold to train or evaluate models as 'past papers' or 'internal question banks' did not come from it, and that it never tested any model.
learn.explanation: A score on an exam-style benchmark only measures generalisation if the test items, or close paraphrases, were not in the training data. The standard first check is n-gram overlap: tokenise each test item, take its set of long n-grams (13 words is a common choice) and measure what fraction also appear in the training corpus; items above a threshold are flagged and the score is reported on the clean subset as well. Long n-grams make chance matches rare, so high overlap almost always means the item was seen. It misses paraphrases, translations and reformatted questions, which need embedding similarity or model-based probes such as checking whether the model completes a question verbatim or prefers the original over a reworded version. When the training data is unknown, as with a vendor claim, the honest move is to evaluate on fresh items written after the model's cutoff. The strings below are toy examples.
learn.python:
# Benchmark contamination check: share of each test item's word 13-grams that also
# appear in a training corpus. Toy strings, illustrative only.
def ngrams(text, n=13):
    w = text.lower().split()
    return {tuple(w[i:i + n]) for i in range(len(w) - n + 1)}

train_docs = [
    "a patient presents with fever thirst and a rapid floating pulse which pattern "
    "best describes the presentation according to the classical texts on exterior conditions",
    "unrelated web text about stock markets and chips falling sharply in a broad sell off "
    "across asia on friday afternoon trading sessions",
]
test_items = [
    "q1: a patient presents with fever thirst and a rapid floating pulse which pattern "
    "best describes the presentation according to the classical texts",
    "q2: a patient reports chronic fatigue cold limbs and a deep slow pulse what is "
    "the most appropriate treatment principle in this case",
]
train_grams = set().union(*(ngrams(d) for d in train_docs))
for item in test_items:
    g = ngrams(item)
    overlap = len(g & train_grams) / max(1, len(g))
    flag = "CONTAMINATED" if overlap > 0.5 else "clean"
    print(f"{item[:3]} 13-gram overlap {overlap:.0%} -> {flag}")
